newsitem.title: USA: Clinton faces questions on political funds uproar.
newsitem.headline: Clinton faces questions on political funds uproar.

text.p: President Bill Clinton prepared to defend controversial campaign fund-raising practices at a news conference on Friday amid heavy pressure for an independent investigation.

Clinton, struggling to pursue his second term agenda of balancing the budget, improving U.S. education and carrying out a tough new welfare law despite the political financing uproar, was scheduled to meet reporters in the White House East Room Friday afternoon at 2 p.m. EST (1900 GMT).
Aides said he would open with a statement on the economy and on what he is doing to help veterans afflicted with mysterious illnesses after duty in the 1991 Gulf War.

Asked how the fund-raising furore was affecting the trouble-prone president -- who also faces a sexual harrassment lawsuit and a continuing probe of business and ethical dealings dating from his days as Arkansas governor -- White House spokesman Mike McCurry said: "He's enjoying himself ... He's not going to allow himself to be precoccupied with it."

At his last full-scale question-and-answer session with reporters on Jan. 28, Clinton conceded "mistakes were made" in raising tens of millions of dollars for his 1996 re-election drive. But he said no laws were broken, and that there was no corruption of policymaking in the fund-raising frenzy.

Since then however, there has been a steady stream of disclosures about how he and his top subordinates, including Vice President Al Gore, financed their costly campaign to defeat Republican Bob Dole in last November's election.
Clinton's Democratic Party has returned nearly $3 million to donors -- most of them men with links to Asian businesses or governments -- that were deemed illegal or questionable.
The foreign-influenced contributions stirred questions of whether overseas interests were trying to buy influence over U.S. trade and foreign policy decisions.

The White House says there is no justification for such questions. But its cause was not helped by recent disclosures that Clinton himself enthusiastically approved proposals to invite major campaign cash donors to special White House events including overnight stays in the Lincoln Bedroom.

Possibly more troublesome from a legal standpoint -- and sure to be a focus of questioning -- was Gore's admission on Monday that he dialed for dollars for the Clinton campaign, using a White House telephone to call potential contributors.

The vice president, who enjoyed a squeaky clean image, insisted he broke no law despite a statute that forbids political fund-raising on federal property and a memo from the White House counsel's office underscoring that prohibition.

Headline-writers dubbed Gore the "Solicitor-in-Chief," and editorial writers charged that his fundraising calls were tantamount to a shakedown, arguing that it would be hard for a potential contributor to say no to the vice president.

That flap was followed by a White House admission that Hillary Rodham Clinton's chief of staff, Maggie Williams, took a $50,000 campaign check from a Chinese-American businessman at the White House in 1995.

White House officials insisted Williams was merely an innocent go-between and passed the money right along to the Democratic Party's leadership group. But critics suggested she had broken the law and the White House defence was evasion.

Congressional Republicans are preparing to set up a Senate investigation into the fund-raising controversy. But they are also demanding that Attorney General Janet Reno appoint an independent counsel to run a separate probe that could lead to criminal prosecutions of any wrongdoing alleged.
Reno is resisting but she is coming under heavier political pressure to give in on this point.
She argues that the Justice Department is already looking into the case with a task force that includes 25 FBI agents.
